title: Performance sprint alignment - Kythera Health POC review
customer_attendees: Dr. Priya Natarajan - Head of ML
summary: Week 3 POC alignment: Redwood and Kythera reviewed lab results comparing latency and throughput against incumbent (CloudLex). Key decisions: try a tighter batching window + prefix KV caching, run one final 4-hour throughput stress on dedicated slots, Redwood to share tuned config and cost delta. Customer to provide production-like prompt set and opt-in for p99 tail analysis.
next_steps: Redwood - share tuned config + cost delta spreadsheet by 2026-10-25
Kythera - upload 6k sample production prompts and expected concurrency profile by 2026-10-24
action_items: Maya Chen: send tuned batch policy and cost spreadsheet - 2026-10-25
Liam O'Connor: prepare runbook for 4-hour dedicated stress and include KV prefix test - 2026-10-27
Tom Reyes: share token distribution and 95/99 latency SLAs - 2026-10-24
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-10-21 15:00 UTC | Duration: 46 min
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Natarajan (Kythera Head of ML), Tom Reyes (Platform), Aisha Malik (Product)
Links referenced: onboarding deck (link: https://redwood.company/decks/kythera-poc), bench spreadsheet (link: spreadsheet://kythera-week3), previous run logs (s3://kythera-poc/logs)

[00:00] Maya Chen: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick round robin, then we'll dive into the week three numbers.
[00:12] Priya: hi, Priya here. got Tom and Aisha with me. small scheduling note, we have a board review in two weeks so want to shorten cycles for the run.
[00:22] Tom: Tom, platform eng. I'll be running the dedicated jobs and watching infra.
[00:28] Aisha: hi all. product, focusing on latency SLOs for user flows.
[00:34] Liam O'Connor: Liam from Redwood, I'll walk the engineering diffs and the tuning we tried.

[02:05] Maya: quick recap — last week we saw mixed results vs your incumbent CloudLex: at p50 we beat them, p95 close, p99 tails spiky under burst. Today we'll go through the bench spreadsheet, call out tuning levers, and agree a final run window.

[03:18] Priya: yes the p99 tail is the crux. our users see intermittent laggy completions and it affects our throughput pricing contract. we need consistent tails under 800ms for short prompts, and under 1.8s for long dialogue rounds.

[04:00] Liam: right, we broke this down into three factors in the sheet — batching window, KV (prefix) cache hits, and quantization profile. We also measured cold KV misses vs warmed cache. our inference engine benefits a lot from warmed KV for multi-turns.

[04:45] Tom: can you remind me numbers? like tokens/sec and GPU occupancy for the runs?

[05:00] Liam: sure. baseline run (CloudLex) — their published numbers: p50 ~120 t/s, p95 ~90 t/s, p99 ~70 t/s (for 32k context sim). Our Redwood hosted run w/ default batching: p50 150 t/s, p95 95 t/s, p99 72 t/s. But when concurrency spiked (simulated 250 concurrent sessions) we saw p99 jumps because batching queued longer then flush.

[05:54] Priya: okay so higher p50 but tail noisier. can we trade a bit of p50 for better p99?

[06:10] Liam: yes, the knob is max batch latency and the continuous batching policy. We tried a tighter window (from 20ms to 8ms), which pushed p99 down ~200ms but dropped throughput by ~8-10%. On top of that, prefix KV caching — when warmed — saved another ~120ms on median for multi-turns.

[07:05] Aisha: what about quantization? we saw a small quality delta on the NLU tests when we used 4-bit q8m; was that expected?

[07:20] Liam: we used a mixed profile. For the highest throughput run we tested int8-ish profiles and saw small regressions on intent classification in the eval set — about 0.7% absolute. we can push quality by using a hybrid profile: keep float for the top attention and quant for bulk matmuls. that reduces perf a tad but keeps accuracy.

[09:10] Maya: Priya, when you say production-like prompts, are you talking about short single-turn queries or multi-turn histories?

[09:22] Priya: both. 60% multi-turn (avg 4 turns), 40% short queries. typical token span per request 80 to 400 tokens. we'll upload a representative set.

[10:00] Tom: one operational item — we need to ensure our VPC peering and egress limits don't throttle your dedicated run. last week we hit a NAT gateway quota and had packet drops at peak.

[10:20] Liam: good catch. for the dedicated 4-hour stress we'll provision a direct path and monitor network QPS. We'll also include a fallback route to a secondary region if we see saturation.

[12:05] Maya: let's walk the week-three bench sheet. Liam?

[12:12] Liam: opening sheet - slide reference row 12 to 28. (brief pause) OK, section A: short prompts (<128 tokens). Our tuned config A had batch latency 8ms, batch size avg 28, run on a single A100x2 slot (dedicated). Observed: p50 165 t/s, p95 110 t/s, p99 88 t/s. CloudLex reported p99 95 t/s in their doc. So we're slightly better but not dramatically.

[14:00] Priya: those numbers look promising. how about long prompts?

[14:10] Liam: long prompts (256-512 tokens) — with prefix KV warm, p50 ~85 t/s, p95 60 t/s, p99 50 t/s. Without KV warm, p99 was 190ms worse due to memory lookups and KV repop overhead. our runtime's continuous KV cache helps but first-turn misses are expensive.

[15:05] Tom: is there a way to pre-warm KV on redwood side? like we send a synthetic prefetch?

[15:20] Liam: yes, we added a pre-warm pass that plays back user histories at low priority before peak runs. It cost about 5% extra tokens but shaved p99 by 140ms in our test. We'll include that as an option for the final run.

[16:40] Aisha: any security/regression concerns with pre-warming? we don't want patient data persisted longer than policy allows.

[16:55] Maya: we recommend synthetic anonymized pre-warm — Redwood can accept hashed keys and we can configure TTL on KV entries to 30 minutes for the pre-warm window. That meets most privacy controls. We'll document in the runbook.

[18:10] Priya: on cost — you mentioned a delta vs CloudLex. can we get a rough percent? engineering is okay but procurement needs ballpark.

[18:25] Maya: preliminary numbers: with tuned quant and batching, hosted per-token cost ~12% lower than CloudLex for your workload profile. On dedicated reserved slots the unit cost can drop ~35% depending on utilization and spot capacity. We'll put precise row-level numbers in the spreadsheet.

[19:05] Tom: good. procurement will want sustained throughput and failure modes. if the dedicated slot fails, we need deterministic fallback to baseline to avoid user-facing errors.

[19:22] Liam: absolutely — we have routing policies: primary dedicated, fail-over to regional shared cluster, and last-resort fallback to CloudLex via HTTP proxy if configured. Failover preserves request semantics but may have slightly higher latency. We can instrument a silent fallback for the run to measure user impact.

[20:40] Priya: how frequent were the fallbacks in your earlier stress?

[20:48] Liam: in our synthetic burst where we simulated a 3x traffic spike, failover happened ~0.7% of requests for the 30-minute window because we pushed concurrent slots beyond autoscale threshold. 0.7% is not great but acceptable if it's silent and we alert.

[22:00] Maya: action: for the final 4-hour run we propose increasing autoscale headroom, tighten batching window, enable pre-warm for multi-turns, and run three quant profiles: conservative (hybrid float/quant), aggressive (4-bit), and balanced (our recommendation).

[22:35] Aisha: timeline?

[22:40] Maya: propose run on 2026-10-28. Redwood to share tuned configs by 10/25. Kythera to upload production prompts by 10/24.

[24:05] Tom: a quick deep-dive question — you mentioned p99 spikes tied to queueing delays. is that primarily due to batching latency or GPU kernel stall?

[24:20] Liam: mostly batching queue delay when short-window flushes misalign with burst arrivals. There's also occasional kernel contention when multiple models share the same GPU host (less relevant for dedicated). We've profiled traces — attaching flame graphs in the sheet.

[26:35] Priya: can we run a targeted p99 tail analysis? like instrument timestamps at our app layer and compare to your server-side timestamps to isolate network vs inference cost?

[26:55] Liam: yes, we can add span-level tracing. Redwood will correlate client send time, server ingestion, batch formation, kernel enqueue, and response exit. We'll produce a p95/p99 waterfall.

[28:10] Tom: curious — any surprises in memory usage when you enabled larger KV prefetch?

[28:22] Liam: a little. prefetch increases GPU host memory pressure due to KV heap plus token cache, but with our tuned TTL and evictions it's manageable. For the 8-node run we needed one extra eviction thread, negligible perf cost. We'll include memory charts.

[30:05] Aisha: on quality, the hybrid quant profile gave us ~0.3% drop in intent accuracy? earlier you said 0.7. which is it?

[30:18] Liam: apologies — different eval sets. On short-turn NLU set it's ~0.3, on long dialogue intent set ~0.7. We'll add per-eval-row numbers so you can decide.

[31:40] Priya: one last question on observability — will we have token-level cost and latency breakdowns per route? our billing integrates with that.

[31:55] Maya: yes, Redwood Console will surface per-route token cost and latency percentiles, with export via CSV/BigQuery. We'll give you access to a demo tenant for the final run.

[33:10] Tom: procurement and legal question — we need clarifications around data retention and audit logs for the dedicated slot. can you confirm logs are customer-owned and retention configurable?

[33:28] Maya: yes — audit logs for Dedicated are in your VPC and can be set via retention policy. For Private deployments we offer on-prem options. We'll share the security pack with SOC2/ISO statements.

[35:05] Priya: any risk items we should note before the final run?

[35:12] Liam: risk: NAT/gateway quotas, cold KV misses if the pre-warm fails, and potential tokenization edge cases when prompts include non-UTF characters. Mitigations: monitor egress, run pre-warm validation, and include a tokenization sanity pass on upload.

[36:40] Maya: ok let's confirm decisions: 1) run 4-hour dedicated stress on 10/28; 2) Redwood will test three quant profiles and recommend one; 3) enable pre-warm synthetic playbacks; 4) share cost delta spreadsheet; 5) Kythera provides prompt set and concurrency profile.

[37:10] Aisha: agreed. please also include an executive one-pager we can show the board highlighting cost delta and SLOs.

[37:20] Maya: will do.

[38:45] Tom: small note — if fallback to CloudLex is last resort, procurement wants a playbook for when that happens. can you draft the sequence?

[38:55] Liam: yes — we'll include an automated routing policy doc and a manual escalation flow in the runbook.

[40:10] Priya: any remaining concerns on our end — Tom?

[40:18] Tom: just to ensure the dedicated run doesn't affect dev environment. we'll create a tagged project and VLAN.

[41:05] Maya: perfect. we'll coordinate with you on network ops.

[42:00] (brief side chatter: confirm calendar invites)

[42:30] Maya: recap of next steps (will add to calendar invite): Redwood send tuned configs and cost spreadsheet; Liam sends runbook and flame graphs; Kythera uploads prompts and token distribution; schedule 4-hour run 10/28.

[43:05] Priya: thanks all. appreciate the clear run plan.

[43:12] Aisha: thanks.

[43:18] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in email with attachments.

[43:30] Meeting ends.
